subject: Agriculture
title: The Shrinking Farm Workforce
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Shrinking Farm Workforce.

hook.text: In 1900, 40% of Americans worked on farms. Today it's under 2%. The food output is vastly larger.

buildup.text: Machines, chemicals, and better seeds replaced human labor at every stage of farming.

discovery.text: One American farmer today feeds about 166 people. In 1900, one farmer fed just seven.

twist.text: Rural communities shrank as farming needed fewer hands. Schools, shops, and hospitals closed.

climax.text: Productivity soared, but the human cost was rural depopulation across every industrialized nation.

punchline.text: Farming feeds more with fewer—and empties the countryside.

quiz.question: How many people does one American farmer feed today?

details.summary: The farm workforce has shrunk dramatically over the past century as mechanization, chemicals, and technology replaced human labor. This topic tracks this transition, its social consequences, and the labor challenges modern agriculture still faces.
details.whyItMatters: In 1900, 40% of Americans worked on farms; today it is under 2%. This massive labor shift shaped modern society, built cities, and created both opportunity and displacement for hundreds of millions of people.
takeaways: Mechanization reduced the US farming population from 40% in 1900 to under 2% today
Each US farmer now feeds about 165 people compared to 10 people a century ago
Modern agriculture still depends on seasonal and migrant labor for harvest tasks

faq.question: Why has the farm workforce shrunk so dramatically?
faq.answer: Tractors, combines, chemical herbicides, and modern equipment replaced human and animal labor. Each technological advance required fewer workers, and economic pressure drove consolidation into fewer, larger farms that need minimal labor per acre.

faq.question: What challenges does the shrinking farm workforce create?
faq.answer: Rural communities lose population and services, traditional farming knowledge disappears, remaining farms depend on aging operators, and crops still requiring hand labor face chronic worker shortages that drive interest in robotic harvesting.
